a: as he had told him to go up to the top of the mountain
p: VanderKam's text reports God's words; the EOTC copy quotes them.

readings.plain: as he had told him to go up to the top of the mountain
as he had said to him, "Go up to the top of the mountain"

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's critical text, its base. The meaning is the same.

a: which I have written for you to teach them
p: VanderKam's text: "which I have written." The EOTC copy: "which you have written."

readings.plain: which I have written for you to teach them
which you have written, so that you may teach them

why: "I have written" agrees with Exodus 24:12, where God writes the tablets. The EOTC copy's "you have written" would make Moses the writer of the stone tablets, which Exodus 31:18 and 34:1 deny.
b: Exodus 34:27-28 has Moses write down the words of the covenant, and some readers have mixed the two writings. Here the tablets are meant.

a: the account of the division of all the days, of the law and of the testimony
t: All the days, and the law
p: In VanderKam's text the division is of all the days and of the law; in the EOTC copy it is of the days of the law.

readings.en: (the division of all) the days, and of the law and of the testimony
readings.plain: the account of the division of all the days, of the law and of the testimony

readings.en: (the division of all) the days of the law and the testimony
readings.plain: the account of the division of all the days of the law and of the testimony

why: The Plain English Translation follows its base, VanderKam's text, where the book divides all of time and also gives the law and the testimony, as 1:29 joins "the division of the years" with "the law and the testimony." The EOTC copy ties the days to the law alone. Smaller differences of the EOTC copy in 1:12, 1:15 and 1:17 ("to them" or "upon them," a past or present verb, "God" or "their God") do not change the meaning and have no entry.

a: that I have not abandoned them
p: The EOTC copy lacks the "not": God abandoned them for their evil.

readings.plain: that I have not abandoned them
that I abandoned them

why: Both make sense: God leaves them to their enemies for their sin, or God never leaves them in spite of it. VanderKam's text fits 1:6 ("I have truly been with them") and 1:18 ("I will not abandon them"), so the Plain English Translation follows it. Charles's English also has "I have not forsaken them."

a: I have been more in the right than they
p: VanderKam's verb form reads "they were righteous"; the EOTC copy adds "I."

readings.w: EOTC printed Bible (digital copy), which adds ʾänä "I"; Charles's English (1913) has the same sense
readings.en: that I was righteous, more than they
readings.plain: I have been more in the right than they

readings.en: that (they) were righteous, more than they
readings.plain: they were in the right, more than they,

why: The verb in VanderKam's text is a plural form ("they were righteous"), which gives no clear sense beside "more than they" and the next clause, "I have truly been with them." The EOTC copy supplies "I," and Charles's English reads "I am more righteous than they." The Plain English Translation follows that sense.

a: They will make themselves high places
p: VanderKam's text has two past-tense verbs in the prophecy; the EOTC copy has future ones. The Plain English Translation follows the EOTC copy here.

readings.en: they will make; likewise wäysägdu, they will bow down
readings.plain: They will make themselves high places

readings.en: they made; likewise wäsägädu, they bowed down
readings.plain: They made themselves high places

why: The verbs around them in God's speech (1:10, 1:12-14) are future, and Charles's English has "they will make" and "they will worship." The past forms may be a prophet's way of speaking of what is sure to happen, but in English they would break the prophecy, so the Plain English Translation departs from its base here and keeps the future with the EOTC copy.

a: hunt down those who search out the law
t: Hunted down, or killed and hunted
p: The EOTC copy adds "kill": they will kill and hunt down those who search out the law.

readings.plain: hunt down those who search out the law

readings.en: they will kill them and drive them out
readings.plain: kill and hunt down those who search out the law

why: VanderKam's text has only the verb "drive out" or "persecute." The EOTC copy's extra "kill" repeats the killing of the witnesses just before.

t: Go wrong about, or do away with
p: The EOTC copy says they will do away with the start of the month, the Sabbaths and the feasts.

readings.plain: They will go wrong about
They will do away with

why: VanderKam's "err" fits the book's charge that Israel will keep the feasts on the wrong days (6:34-38), not that it will stop keeping them. Charles's English has "go astray as to new moons."

t: "Write for yourself" or "I will write for you"
p: Two of Charles's four manuscripts have God say, "I will write down for you."

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's manuscripts b and c (Charles 1902, note on 1:26)
readings.plain: Write down for yourself

readings.w: Charles's manuscripts a and d (Charles 1902, note on 1:26)
readings.en: and I will write down for you
readings.plain: I will write down for you

why: The command to Moses matches 1:5 and 1:7. The other reading would make God the writer, which does not fit 1:27, where God tells the angel to write.

a: They run from the day of the new creation, when
t: From the new creation, or from creation until
p: Charles thought "new" and "when" were errors and that the tablets run from creation until the renewal.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's own text and English (1913)
readings.orig: እምዕለተ ፍጥረት ሐዳስ አመ (ʾəmʿəlätä fəṭrät ḥädas ʾämä)
readings.en: from the day of the new creation when
readings.plain: They run from the day of the new creation, when

readings.w: A correction proposed by Charles 1902 (note on 1:29), found in no manuscript: "new" an Ethiopic addition, and "when" from Greek ὡς misread for ἕως, "until"
readings.en: from the day of creation until
readings.plain: They run from the day of creation until

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez as it stands. Charles's correction gives a clearer sense (the tablets cover all history from creation to the renewal) but has no manuscript support.

t: Angels of holiness or of glory
p: Epiphanius' Greek has "angels of glory" where the Ge'ez has "angels of holiness."

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); the same phrase at 15:27, where the Latin has sanctificationis (Charles 1902)
readings.plain: the angels of holiness

readings.w: Greek, Epiphanius, On Weights and Measures 22, as cited in Charles 1902
readings.plain: the angels of glory

why: Charles 1902 defends the Ge'ez because the Latin at 15:27 also has "of sanctification." The Greek "angels of glory" may mean angels who give glory, close in sense to the Ge'ez.

a: of darkness and of all things
p: Epiphanius' Greek lists angels "of snow" here; the Ge'ez has a word meaning "all."

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989) (with Charles's manuscripts a and b)
readings.plain: of darkness and of all things

readings.w: Greek, Epiphanius, On Weights and Measures 22, as cited in Charles 1902, followed in Charles's English
readings.plain: of darkness, of snow

why: Charles 1902 thought the Greek word for snow was misread as "all" before the Ethiopic translation was made, and he follows the Greek. The Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam's Ge'ez, its base, and gives the Greek here; the list goes on with hail and frost, which supports Charles.

t: "For delight and for all" or "all plants after their kind"
p: Charles replaced the unclear Ge'ez words with "all plants after their kind" from the Greek of Epiphanius.

readings.plain: for delight and for all

readings.w: Epiphanius, as cited in Charles 1902; Charles's English (1913)
readings.orig: καὶ πάντα τὰ φυτὰ κατὰ γένος
readings.en: and all the plants according to their kind
readings.plain: and all plants after their kind

why: Charles 1902 judged the Ge'ez damaged here and supplied the words from the Greek. The Plain English Translation keeps its base, the Ge'ez, and says in a note that it is unclear.

a: There were twenty-two heads of humankind from Adam down to him, and twenty-two kinds of work were made
p: Greek writers who used Jubilees show that something is missing here: the twenty-two Hebrew letters and books.

readings.orig: ዕሥራ ወክልኤ አርእስተ ሰብእ እምአዳም እስከኔሁ (ʿəśra wäkləʾe ʾärʾəstä säbʾ ʾəmʾädam ʾəskänehu)
readings.en: twenty-two heads of humankind from Adam until him
readings.plain: There were twenty-two heads of humankind from Adam down to him, and twenty-two kinds of work were made

readings.w: Restoration proposed by Charles 1902 from Epiphanius (On Weights and Measures 22), Syncellus and Cedrenus
readings.orig: καὶ εἴκοσι δύο κεφάλαια ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ ἄχρι τοῦ Ἰακώβ (Epiphanius)
readings.en: As there were twenty-two letters and twenty-two (sacred) books and twenty-two heads of humankind from Adam to Jacob, so there were made twenty-two kinds of work
readings.plain: As there were twenty-two letters, twenty-two sacred books and twenty-two heads of humankind from Adam to Jacob, so twenty-two kinds of work were made

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez, the only full text. Charles 1902 shows that Epiphanius, after retelling the creation from this book, says the angel told Moses of "twenty-two heads from Adam to Jacob," and links them to the twenty-two Hebrew letters and the twenty-two books of the Hebrew Bible; Syncellus says the same, "as it is told in the Little Genesis." So the full text may once have named the letters and the books. Verse 22 seems to break off in mid-sentence ("all the days..."), which supports a gap.
b: The "twenty-two books" is an old Jewish way of counting the Hebrew Bible: Charles explains that the Twelve prophets count as one book, and Judges with Ruth, Ezra with Nehemiah, Jeremiah with Lamentations, and the two books each of Samuel, Kings and Chronicles are joined.

a: a daughter of his father's sister
p: The Ge'ez says the patriarchs married daughters of their father's sister. Charles changed it to "father's brother."

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's manuscripts (Charles 1902, note on 4:15)
readings.plain: a daughter of his father's sister

readings.w: Charles's correction (Charles 1902, 1913), from the Syriac list of the patriarchs' wives, the Greek manuscript r of Genesis 5:15 (πατραδέλφου αὐτοῦ) and Epiphanius, Panarion 39.7
readings.plain: a daughter of his father's brother

why: Charles 1902 says his manuscripts read "father's sister" and that he corrected it to "father's brother" from the Syriac and Greek witnesses, and that he makes the same correction in the later cases except 8:6 and 11:7. The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez, its base. The same phrase stands in 4:16, 4:20, 4:27 and 4:28.

a: Because of him the waters of the Flood did not come on any of the land of Eden
p: VanderKam's text: the Flood did not reach Eden, because Enoch was there. Charles's English: God brought the Flood on Eden.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); the EOTC digital copy agrees
readings.orig: ወበእንቲአሁ ኢመጽአ ማየ አይኅ (wäbäʾnətiʾähu ʾimäṣʾä mayä ʾäyḫ)
readings.en: because of him the water of the Flood did not come
readings.plain: Because of him the waters of the Flood did not come on any of the land of Eden

readings.w: Charles's English (1902, 1913), from his edition of the Ge'ez
readings.en: on account of it (God) brought the waters of the flood upon all the land of Eden
readings.plain: Because of this the waters of the Flood came on all the land of Eden

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's critical text. The two readings differ by one word, the Ge'ez "not." With it, Eden is spared because Enoch, the righteous scribe, lives there; without it, the Flood comes on Eden too. Charles 1902 compared 2 Enoch 34:3, "on this account I will bring a deluge."

a: on the Mountain of the South
p: Most manuscripts name a mountain with the word qatr, "south" or "midday." Charles read it as "sweet spices."

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's manuscripts b, c, d (Charles 1902, note on 4:25)
readings.en: on the mountain of qatr (of the south, or of midday)
readings.plain: on the Mountain of the South

readings.w: Charles's manuscript a, and Charles's English
readings.plain: on the mountain

why: Charles 1902 notes that this use of qatr is found nowhere else; he took it as a corruption of a word for "sweet spices" (Exodus 30:7) and followed manuscript a for "on the mount." The Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam's Ge'ez. Which mountain is meant is unclear; it may be the Mountain of the East of 4:26.

p: Here VanderKam's Ge'ez says Emzara was the daughter of Noah's sister. Charles reads "father's brother."

readings.plain: a daughter of his sister
a daughter of his father's brother

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's Ge'ez as it stands. In 4:15-28 the same formula has "his father's sister"; here "father's" is missing. Charles 1902 corrected the phrase to "father's brother" at every place on the evidence of the Syriac and Greek (see 4:15).
